name: SWE-Gym
description: SWE-Gym is a training environment for software engineering agents containing 2,438 real-world Python task instances, each comprising a codebase with a pre-configured executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a natural language task sourced from GitHub issues. The paper also describes SWE-Gym Lite with 230 instances and SWE-Gym Raw with 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed from real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests and GitHub issues in Python repositories. The authors first used SEART GitHub search to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. They then used SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances containing the issue description, repository snapshot, and unit tests, yielding 64,689 instances as SWE-Gym Raw. They focused on 11 repositories with numerous instances and semi-manually created executable environments for them. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using repository configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation, and SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to verify that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering failed instances, 2,438 unit-test-validated instances remained. SWE-Gym Lite was created by following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline to select 230 easier, more self-contained tasks.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data sources were GitHub repositories, GitHub issues, pull requests, repository snapshots, unit tests, repository configuration files such as pyproject.toml and requirements.txt, CI scripts, documentation, git tags, and other repository version information. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 Python GitHub issues spanning 358 Python repositories without executable environments.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories were selected from those created before July 1, 2022.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors generalized SWE-Bench's versioning script to support versioning via script execution and semi-automatically collected versions for each instance based on repository information such as pyproject.toml and git tags. They associated instances with version numbers, set up environments version-by-version, validated instances using execution-based checks, and filtered out failed instances. SWE-Gym Lite further excluded tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, tasks with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each repository was converted into task instances using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. For selected repositories, executable environments were created by manually configuring dependencies from requirements.txt, CI scripts, or repository documentation at the time of issue creation. The authors then used SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the human gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code, and filtered out failed instances. Pre-built Docker images were released for each validated instance for reproducibility.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset uses expert-validated test cases and human-submitted gold patches from pull requests. During environment construction, the authors manually configured dependencies for each task instance and validated whether the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. The paper states this process required approximately 200 human annotation hours. For verifier training, trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful based on whether unit tests indicated the problem was solved, and models were fine-tuned to predict success labels such as <YES>/<NO> or True/False.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors used execution-based validation to ensure that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code and filtered out failed instances. They also discuss easy-task bias in sampled successful trajectories: repeated sampling showed a long-tail success distribution, and they introduced per-instance capping to limit the maximum number of selected successful samples per task to mitigate bias toward easier tasks. For verifier training, they balanced successful and unsuccessful trajectories and found that mixing on-policy and off-policy data improved verifier performance.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script, SWE-Bench's versioning script, SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script, unit-test-based success labeling, SGLang, Unsloth, torchtune
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they publicly release SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, pre-built Docker images for each instance, and open source all artifacts of the project including dataset, model weights, agent trajectory data, and the training pipeline. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is specified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries, support critical open-source infrastructure, and make software development more accessible. It also notes potential impacts on software engineering jobs and the need for consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. The authors warn that similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code and encourage future work on responsible deployment, including security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes several biases. Manually configuring executable environments was intended to avoid distribution bias that could arise from ignoring complex environments. The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total and bokeh about one percent. The authors also identify easy-data bias in successful sampled trajectories, where broader task coverage introduces bias toward easier tasks; they mitigate this with per-instance capping. They further note that approaches that simply discard instances failing setup may bias environments away from tasks with complex dependencies.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that SWE-Gym is limited by environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. SWE-Gym contains only Python tasks from 11 repositories with executable environments, while SWE-Gym Raw lacks executable environments and guarantees that unit tests effectively evaluate correctness. The authors also note that current models are primarily research artifacts and not yet production-ready. They report that self-improvement results are modest and that verifier performance is imperfect, leaving a gap between Pass@k and Best@k.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a training environment for software engineering agents and verifiers. The paper uses SWE-Gym to train language-model-based SWE agents through rejection sampling fine-tuning and self-improvement experiments, and to train verifier/reward models on agent trajectories for inference-time scaling and trajectory reranking. SWE-Gym Lite is described as suitable for rapid prototyping. The dataset is also released to support future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
